channelDescription: Fitness made simple.

text:
Why does your ab workout hurt your back instead of building abs? I break down the real reason you’re not seeing gains, and why your lower back is taking all the damage. If you’re doing leg raises and feeling more pain than progress, you’re likely overusing your hip flexors, not your abs. Specifically, a deep muscle called the psoas is doing all the work, yanking on your spine and sabotaging your results.
Your abs are built to flex your spine, pulling your ribcage toward your pelvis. So what is the real fix? It’s all about spine flexion. If you curl the bottom of your spine, you will disengage your hip flexors, and finally get your abs to contract. One of the best ways to learn this movement? Start on a bench. Training on a slight incline helps you reduce psoas activation, making it easier to isolate the abs and really focus on that spinal flexion.
In this video I show you exactly how to do that to get actual ab activation. Say goodbye to back pain and start building real core strength the right way.

text:
The triceps is the arm muscle that decides how full your arm looks when it's doing nothing — just hanging at your side, not flexed. Here's why the triceps long head builds the horseshoe, why it's two-thirds of the arm, and how the dumbbell close-grip press carves it.

Most of the arm only shows up when it works. Flex it, pump it, and it fills — twenty minutes later it's gone. The triceps doesn't play by that rule. Trained heavy, it stays carved when the arm is dead at your side. That's the arm you actually wear all day. Not the one you pose for five seconds in a mirror.

The shape is the horseshoe — a thick sweep curving down the back of the arm, edges sharp enough to trace. And the triceps is two-thirds of the arm, so the back of the arm is where the size actually comes from. Train it like the bigger muscle it is and the whole arm grows with it.

The move is the dumbbell close-grip press. Flat on a bench, a dumbbell in each hand, knuckles almost touching — and they stay that close the entire set. That narrow grip drags the work onto the back of the arm and off the chest. Elbows tucked tight, never flared. Lower slow to the middle of the chest, then drive up and lock the arms out hard at the top. That lockout is the rep — the part that builds the sweep. Most guys stop just short of it and quietly cut the range in half. Full lockout, every rep, as heavy as you can press while holding that grip tight.

Three things that separate a built triceps from a trained one:

— Load the stretch. The long head grows hardest at the bottom — arm overhead or elbow behind the body. Overhead extensions and deep dips hit what pressdowns miss.

— Lock every rep. The last few degrees of lockout is pure long head. Half reps build half an arm.

— Pressdowns are a finisher, not the main course. They pump the outer head but leave the mass — the long head — undertrained. Press and extend heavy first, isolate last.

#triceps #armday

When you do regular squats, your stronger leg usually takes over and your weaker side just survives the reps. text:
Are you trying to grow your glutes but not seeing real results? If you're chasing the “muscle burn” instead of following proven training science, you might be wasting your time. In this complete guide to glute growth, I break down exactly how to build strong, round, and well-developed glutes using evidence-based principles — and we’ll debunk the popular gluteal amnesia myth once and for all.

To build bigger glutes, you must understand glute anatomy. The glutes consist of three muscles: the gluteus maximus (the largest and most powerful), the gluteus medius, and the gluteus minimus. These muscles are responsible for hip extension, hip abduction, external rotation, and posterior pelvic tilt. If your workout program doesn’t train all of these functions, you’re leaving serious growth on the table.

In this video, you’ll learn the five essential categories of glute exercises that maximize muscle growth and strength:

• Deep stretch movements like squats, lunges, and split squats to load the glutes in hip flexion
• Hinge exercises like Romanian deadlifts (RDLs) to maximize stretch under tension
• Peak contraction exercises such as hip thrusts and glute bridges for maximum shortening and power
• Isolation exercises like kickbacks to target the glutes without excessive fatigue
• Abduction and external rotation exercises to develop the upper and side glutes for a complete, round shape

We also cover how to properly structure your glute workout program using progressive overload, the ideal rep range (6–20 reps), and how close to train to failure for optimal hypertrophy. Whether your goal is stronger glutes, better athletic performance, improved posture, or building a round and well-shaped lower body, this video gives you the blueprint.

And what about gluteal amnesia? Does sitting really make your glutes “turn off”? Not exactly. Sitting does not deactivate your muscles. Weak glutes are simply the result of not training them effectively. You don’t need endless activation drills — you need smart programming and proper execution.

title: Why Khabib Nurmagomedov Never Gets Tired in a Fight
text:
Have you ever wondered why Khabib Nurmagomedov seemed to have an endless gas tank inside the cage? In this video, we explore the science behind elite endurance in mixed martial arts and reveal one of the most powerful training methods used by world-class fighters: high-altitude training.

Khabib’s legendary cardio was not an accident. It was the result of a brutal and highly disciplined training philosophy developed by his father and coach, Abdulmanap Nurmagomedov. Fighters in the Nurmagomedov camp often trained deep in the mountains of Dagestan, at altitudes close to 2,000 meters above sea level, where the oxygen level is significantly lower than at sea level.

Training in this environment forces the human body to undergo powerful physiological adaptations. When oxygen becomes scarce, the body increases the production of erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone that stimulates the creation of more red blood cells. This increases hemoglobin levels, allowing the blood to transport oxygen more efficiently to working muscles.

Over time, these adaptations dramatically improve aerobic capacity, endurance, and recovery speed. This is why fighters who train at altitude often feel stronger, faster, and less fatigued when they return to lower elevations.

Inside the cage, these adaptations become a massive advantage. While many opponents begin to slow down from exhaustion, Khabib was famous for maintaining relentless pressure for all five rounds. His ability to grapple, control, and dominate opponents without slowing down became one of the defining characteristics of his fighting style.

But this video is not just about Khabib. It’s about understanding the science of stamina, oxygen efficiency, and endurance training that athletes, fighters, and even everyday fitness enthusiasts can learn from.

If you want to improve your cardio, stamina, and athletic performance, understanding how the body adapts to stress, oxygen demand, and training intensity is essential. The principles discussed in this video apply not only to MMA fighters but also to athletes, runners, and anyone serious about physical performance.
